chrome_launch.description: How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)

exclude.description: Profiles to exclude when using --profile all (comma delimited); alias: --e; use 'none' or an empty string to clear configured defaults

headed.description: Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

headless.description: Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

ignore_risk.description: Run this once even if your Risk Profile would hold it (a daily cap, quiet hours, outreach turned off or a pause after a sign-in challenge). Only this run; your Risk Profile stays as it is. A limit the platform itself publishes still applies

limit.description: Maximum acceptances confirmed in one run. A click is not an acceptance: only an invitation confirmed gone from the received list counts, and an invitation skipped because LinkedIn warned about it never consumes the budget. 0 means no limit (the run stops at the examination ceiling).

log_dir.description: Directory where daily rotated stdout/stderr logs are persisted while still streaming to the console

pace.description: Pace of the random delays between 'blowhorn accept' actions (page loads, typing, clicks, API calls): a preset name (fast/normal/slow) or a numeric multiplier (e.g. 0.5, 2.0). Resolved as CLI flag, then BLOWHORN_PACE, then defaults.pace in .blowhorn.yaml (normal when none is set); an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs

platform.description: Platform scope for 'blowhorn accept'. One of: linkedin, all ('all' means every platform listed here)

profile.description: Profile context (name, comma-delimited names, or 'all' alias for all profiles)

risk_profile.description: Risk Profile this run uses: cautious, standard or brisk. For this one run it beats the schedule's value, the profile's choice and configuration. A value after the command word wins over one before it; an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs

AcceptRequest.title: AcceptRequest

AcceptResponse.description:
What `blowhorn accept --json` prints on exit 0: the received invitations
the run examined as profile URLs, how many it accepted, and how many it
skipped. A row never carries a display name: identity is the profile URL
only, so no person's name lands in a committed artifact. A flagged
invitation ("Take care when connecting") is skipped, never confirmed: the
warning's own confirm control is never clicked. On a dry run `sent` is 0
and `candidates` are the rows a real run would accept; the preview cannot
know which invitation would raise the warning, because LinkedIn raises it
only after Accept is clicked, so a dry run lists every candidate and says
so rather than promising none would be skipped.

accepted.description: Invitations confirmed accepted, the same count as `sent`.

candidates.description: The received invitations the run examined, as profile URLs, in list order.

profile_url.description: The inviter's LinkedIn profile URL. Never a display name.

dry_run.description: True when nothing was clicked and nothing was written.

examined.description: Rows examined, including rows left unanswered.

failed.description: Rows whose acceptance failed after the control was clicked.

held.description: Rows held as clicked with the outcome not read. Acceptance records none of its own; the list is empty unless a held row was carried in.

sent.description: Invitations confirmed accepted. Always 0 on a dry run.

skipped.description: Rows examined and left unanswered (flagged, stuck, unactionable, unidentifiable, or unreadable).

unconfirmed.description: Rows clicked whose acceptance could not be confirmed from the list.

AcceptResponse.title: AcceptResponse

ActivityDelivery.description:
Mirrors meshery/schemas v1beta3 `ActivityDelivery`. Whether the activity went out for one profile
and platform, from the content item's recorded outcome and the run log. Measured, never derived.

computer.description: Host name of the computer whose run delivered or attempted it.

command.description: A command line that performs the fix, when there is one.

summary.description: One plain sentence saying what to do next.

logPath.description: Log file of the matched run, on the computer that ran it.

status.description: delivered, unconfirmed (clicked, outcome not read), failed (last attempt failed), scheduled, pending (due, not yet run), draft (not approved).

ActivityDelivery.title: ActivityDelivery

ActivityFollowerChange.description:
Mirrors meshery/schemas v1beta3 `ActivityFollowerChange`. Derived: followers at the reading before
the activity and the first reading at least `windowDays` after it. Correlation only.
ActivityFollowerChange.title: ActivityFollowerChange

ActivityMetrics.description:
Mirrors meshery/schemas v1beta3 `ActivityMetrics`. Per-activity engagement figures. The known
keys are always present and are null when the source did not report them, never zero. A
platform-specific figure not listed here is carried under its own key only when reported.

clickThroughRate.description: Clicks divided by impressions, as a fraction.

engagementRate.description: Engagements divided by impressions, as a fraction.

ActivityMetrics.title: ActivityMetrics

ActivityReception.description:
Mirrors meshery/schemas v1beta3 `ActivityReception`. Measured reception with the date it was read,
or collected false with a reason and one sentence. Never zeros for missing data. `comparison` is
derived: the median of the same subject's other activities and this activity's ratio to it.

subject.description: Account or page the figures belong to.

ActivityReception.title: ActivityReception

AuthStatusRequest.title: AuthStatusRequest

AuthStatusResponse.description: Blowhorn sign-in and entitlement state. The token itself is never printed, only whether one is configured. With --offline every field comes from presence checks: no saved secret is read (so macOS shows no Keychain prompt), no request is made, and attestation is null.

account.description: Who is signed in, for the desktop app's account button and menu. Read from cloud.yaml, where sign-in caches it and a live auth status refreshes it from Blowhorn's own answers, each checked against the meshery/schemas construct Blowhorn consumes (schemas/meshery/consumed.yaml): User and its Preference from GET /api/identity/users/profile, AvailableOrganization from GET /api/identity/orgs, and the organization's Subscription and its Plan from /api/entitlement. So --offline answers it with no secret read and no request. Null when no token is configured. A field Blowhorn did not answer is null. The organization is the one organization_id names: the session's active organization (Preference.selectedOrganizationId when the account is still a member, else the first listed, the same choice the browser session makes), unless BLOWHORN_CLOUD_ORGANIZATION names another.

avatar_url.description: User.avatarUrl (meshery/schemas v1beta2 user), the profile photo in your Blowhorn account.

organization_count.description: How many live organizations the account belongs to, as GET /api/identity/orgs last counted them; more than one offers Switch organization.

organization_name.description: AvailableOrganization.name (meshery/schemas v1beta2 organization) of the organization this status reports.

organizations.description: The account's live organizations (GET /api/identity/orgs, soft-deleted ones left out, up to Blowhorn's page of 100), in Blowhorn's order; Switch organization offers these.

description.description: AvailableOrganization.description (meshery/schemas v1beta2 organization), null when Cloud gave none; shown on hover beside the id to tell two organizations of the same name apart.

plan_name.description: Plan.name (meshery/schemas v1beta3 plan, the PlanName enum) of the organization this status reports, exactly as Blowhorn names it, and Free when Blowhorn answered with no current subscription (every organization is on Free unless one names another plan). Null only when it has never been read for that organization; the app then shows the organization alone.

attestation.description: The cached plan attestation, or null when none has been read.

fetched_at.description: ISO 8601 UTC instant the plan was fetched.

attestation_present.description: Whether a saved plan is held. With --offline, from the Keychain item's attributes only; live, whether attestation is non-null.

checked.description: presence for --offline (attributes only: no secret read, no request); live when the saved plan was read and, when due, refreshed from Blowhorn.

cloud_yaml.description: Path of the cloud.yaml in use, if any.

enforcement.description: The entitlement enforcement mode, or "invalid (<reason>)" when the setting does not parse.

ok.description: False when this computer is not signed in. True when a token is configured and, live, Blowhorn accepted it.

permission_keys.description: Live only: the ids of the permission keys the signed-in session holds in the Blowhorn parent organization (GET /api/identity/orgs/by-domain resolves the parent organization, then GET /api/identity/orgs/{id}/users/keys), which the desktop app's Diagnostics gate matches the Access Diagnostics key id against. Empty when no token is configured or when either read fails: the gate fails closed. Absent from the --offline payload, which makes no request.

previous_account.description: Who was signed in on this computer before the session ended, for the desktop app's returning sign-in screen, which greets that person by name. Read from cloud.yaml, where sign-out removes the account: a name still there with no token configured means the token was lost, removed or has timed out, never that the person signed out. Only the name and email, never the photo or the organizations. Null while a token is configured (account answers then), after a sign-out, and when cloud.yaml names nobody. Answered by --offline too: no secret read, no request.

sign_in_problem.description: Why this computer is not signed in, present only when signed_in is false. no token means none is configured. token refused means Blowhorn answered 401 or 403. unreachable means Blowhorn could not be reached. --offline reports only no token.

signed_in.description: Whether this computer is signed in to Blowhorn.

token_configured.description: Whether a Blowhorn token is configured. The token is never printed.

ChromeAttachChromeResponse.description:
Prints the dedicated attach-chrome tree (a second Chrome with the debugging port open, never the
daily one) or what an action did to it. `status`, `start`, `signin` and `stop --dry-run` report

argv.description: The command line that starts (or would start) Chrome; present on `start` and `signin`.

debugging.description: Present on `signin`, which opens the tree with no debugging port.

held_without_debugging.description: True when a live Chrome holds the tree with no debugging port open.

holder_pid.description: The live process holding the tree's SingletonLock, if any.

minimum_version.description: The oldest Chrome major Blowhorn supports.

next_steps.description: What to do after a real `start`, or after `signin`.

plan.description: What a real `stop` would do; present on `stop --dry-run`.

stale_port.description: True when a port is recorded but no live Chrome holds the tree.

started.description: Present on `status`, `start` and `signin`; true only after a real `start` or `signin`.

supported.description: Whether version is at least minimum_version; null when the version is unknown.

plist.description: The LaunchAgent written (or that would be written) to `path`.

ChromeBinding.description:
A Blowhorn profile mapped to a Chrome profile directory on one machine. A mapping is identity, not
permission. A profile may map several Chrome profiles on one machine; a Chrome profile belongs to at
most one Blowhorn profile there. A `--dry-run` preview carries only the first four fields and
`platforms`.

directory.description: The Chrome profile directory name, such as Profile 5.

platforms.description:
The platforms a run uses this Chrome profile for. Empty makes it the profile's default: it serves
every platform none of the profile's other Chrome profiles on this machine names.

profile.description: The Blowhorn profile slug.

ChromeConfirmResponse.description:
One result per assignment `chrome confirm` was given on stdin, in the document's order:
the Blowhorn profile each Chrome profile now posts as, whether confirm created it, the
credential keys it wrote per platform (key names only, never a value), and how the Chrome
profile mapping stands. `ok` is true when at least one assignment landed; a refused
assignment carries its reason in its own row and does not stop the others. The assignments
document itself, typed secrets included, arrives on stdin and is never echoed back.

host.description: The machine host the mappings are keyed by.

ok.description: True when at least one assignment landed.

accounts.description: The accounts this assignment recorded in your Blowhorn account - each attached platform's username, then the browser sign-ins it attached; empty for a dry run, a refusal, or a store that keeps no accounts.

created.description: Confirm created the profile in your Blowhorn account in this run.

directory.description: The Chrome profile directory the assignment named.

error.description: Why this assignment was refused, or null when it landed.

mapped.description: mapped - the mapping was written now; already - it already named this profile; would map - a dry run's answer; null when the assignment was refused before mapping, or when the Chrome profile was recorded not in use and no mapping was written.

notes.description: Follow-ups the write could not finish itself, such as capturing a Slack session interactively.

pairing.description: The pairing a mapping starts, or a mapping confirmed again re-starts, as 'chrome map' reports it, when the extension is already on in that Chrome profile; null when nothing was mapped (including a dry run) or the extension is not on there yet, which the desktop's setup pairs once it is (or 'chrome map'). When the page could not open, a note says how to pair.

detail.description: Why the page was not opened, or null.

opened.description: Chrome was asked to open the pairing page in the mapped Chrome profile. Pairing is done once the page says so.

profile.description: The Blowhorn profile the Chrome profile posts as; null when the assignment was refused before a profile was settled.

written.description: Credential key names written, per platform - names only, never a value.

ChromeConfirmStdinRequest.description:
The JSON document `chrome confirm --payload-stdin` reads. One assignment per Chrome
profile the person decided about. `in_use: false` records that Chrome profile as not
in use. A platform object with `attach: false` records that platform as not in use
on the Blowhorn profile. Neither choice deletes a profile or a credential. A GitHub
token and a Bluesky app password travel in this request and are never echoed.
Only `assignments` and, in each assignment, `directory` are required: the handler
defaults every other field when it is omitted, and it ignores fields it does not
name, at every level of the document. The one exception is an assignment's `email`
or `subject`, which the handler refuses by name: they named a profile's person
before `userId` did, and read as absent they would create a brand where the caller
meant a person.

create.description: Create the profile `profile` names (or the one proposed from the Chrome profile's name) in your Blowhorn account. A profile the organization does not have is never created without it.

directory.description: The Chrome profile directory, as `chrome profiles` prints it.

in_use.description: False records this Chrome profile as not in use. Omitted means in use, so an older document that only lists chosen rows still applies those rows.

app_password.description: Bluesky only. The app password. Travels on stdin, never argv, and is never echoed.

attach.description: False records the platform as not in use. True writes the keys this object carries. Omitted means the platform is not attached.

session.description: LinkedIn or Hacker News. Store a confirmed-session credential naming this Chrome profile instead of a password.

token.description: GitHub only. The personal access token. Travels on stdin, never argv, and is never echoed.

platforms.description: Platform id to the choice for that platform. A platform left out is not changed. Omitted means no platform is changed.

profile.description: An existing Blowhorn profile by name, or the name of the profile to create when `create` is set.

profileId.description: An existing Blowhorn profile, by its id as `profile list` prints it. Never with `create`.

userId.description: Create only. The member of the organization the new profile represents, as `org members` lists them. Omitted creates a brand.

ChromeCreateProfileRequest.description: The flags and arguments of `blowhorn chrome create-profile`, one property per parameter.

chrome_launch.description: How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)

exclude.description: Profiles to exclude when using --profile all (comma delimited); alias: --e; use 'none' or an empty string to clear configured defaults

headed.description: Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

headless.description: Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

json_output.description: Emit the report as JSON with a stable shape, for a script or the desktop app

log_dir.description: Directory where daily rotated stdout/stderr logs are persisted while still streaming to the console

pace.description: Accepted by 'blowhorn chrome create-profile' because --pace is a global flag, but this command does no paced work -- it sleeps between nothing -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs and appears only in the Pace column of the -v summary. Resolved as CLI flag, then BLOWHORN_PACE, then defaults.pace in .blowhorn.yaml (normal when none is set); an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs

platform.description: Accepted and ignored by 'blowhorn chrome': this command never acts on a platform, so --platform has no effect here -- including a value inherited from BLOWHORN_PLATFORM or defaults.platform in .blowhorn.yaml

profile.description: Profile context (name, comma-delimited names, or 'all' alias for all profiles)

risk_profile.description: Accepted by 'blowhorn chrome create-profile' because --risk-profile is a global flag, but this command does no gated work -- no Risk Profile hold, cap or pace applies to it -- so the value changes nothing about how it runs. A value after the command word wins over one before it; an unrecognized value is rejected before anything runs

ChromeCreateProfileResponse.description: What chrome create-profile prints with --json: the Chrome profile directory Blowhorn asked Google Chrome to open a window in, whether Local State already listed it, and whether Chrome was asked to open it. Chrome creates a new profile for a directory it does not know and opens the existing one otherwise, so a repeat never makes a second profile; that was probed live on 2026-10-28 (Google Chrome 156 on macOS). Nothing after the open is read back, so whether Chrome created the profile on a given run is not claimed. A refusal (Google Chrome not installed) prints a Problem instead.

detail.description: Why the window did not open ('chrome could not open blowhorn's chrome profile: <reason>'), or the dry-run note; null when it opened.

directory.description: The Chrome profile directory Blowhorn works in, as chrome profiles prints it once Chrome has created it.

ok.description: Chrome was asked to open the window (always true on a dry run); false with exit 1 when it could not be asked.

opened.description: Chrome was asked to open the window in this profile.

url.description: The page the window opened on.

ChromeDiscoverResponse.description:
The `chrome profiles` rows, plus what setup's confirm step needs for each: the platform
accounts discovery found in that Chrome profile (a saved-login username, or the live
GitHub username; a signed-in flag from a session cookie's presence, never its value),
how the profile's Google email resolves under the profile create rule, and the profile
name a create would propose. Nothing is written to Chrome. For each Chrome profile mapped
here, in use, whose identity holds, the LinkedIn, X and Reddit sign-ins it is picked for
are recorded as the profile's accounts in your Blowhorn account (`accounts`); `--local` and
`--dry-run` record nothing. A not-in-use
row whose directory Chrome no longer has is dropped. Account names are real people's; never
commit a real output.

account_errors.description: One sentence per account the store refused to record, naming the profile and platform.

accounts.description: What this survey recorded in your Blowhorn account, one entry per profile and browser platform it checked.

host.description: The machine host the mappings are keyed by.

last_used.description: Directory of the profile Chrome last used.

local.description: True for `--local`, which reads Chrome's files only, never the store, so nobody is resolved or mapped.

account.description: Signed-in Google account email, empty when nobody is signed in.

identity.description: Whether the recorded identity of the mapping still holds (for example ok or drift); null when unmapped.

in_use.description: False when this Chrome profile was recorded not in use. True only when a record says it is in use. Absent when no choice was recorded.

mapped_to.description: The Blowhorn profile mapped to this Chrome profile on this host.

platforms.description: One entry per platform discovery looks for; a username is a saved login's username or, for GitHub, the live account cookie's value when signed in.

proposed_slug.description: The profile name a create would propose, from the Chrome profile's display name; null when nothing usable can be proposed.

resolution.description: The create rule's answer for the profile's Google email, without creating anything.

socials.description: The resolved user's Cloud social links, for display on the confirm step only; a link is never permission to post.

candidates.description: The organization members holding the email; the confirm step's picker chooses between them.

detail.description: The create rule's refusal sentence, which says what would fix it.

state.description: `--local`: the store was not read, so the email was not resolved.

slug_state.description: Whether the proposed name is free, already the resolved user's own profile, taken by another profile, or not a usable name; unchecked under `--local`.

ChromeDiscoveredPlatform.description:
What discovery found for one platform in one Chrome profile: the account name from a
saved login (or, for GitHub, the live account cookie's value when signed in), and
whether a live session is present - read from a session cookie's presence, never its
value. No password and no cookie value is ever read.

in_use.description: False when this platform was recorded not in use for the profile this Chrome profile posts as. True only when a record says so. Absent when no choice was recorded.

signed_in.description: A live session is present in this Chrome profile.

token_saved.description: GitHub only. True when this Chrome profile's Blowhorn profile already has GH_TOKEN stored. The token itself is never included. Absent on the other platforms.

username.description: The account name discovery found, or null when it found none.

chrome_launch.description: How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)

headed.description: Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

headless.description: Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)

ended here, and `detail` says why.

ProfilePayloadStdinRequest.description:
The JSON document `profile create --payload-stdin` and `profile update --payload-stdin`
read: the v1beta3 `ProfilePayload` fields a person sets. Blowhorn adds `organizationId`;
`owner` and `metadata` are never taken from this document. Any other key is refused. On
an update the document is the whole of these fields: a `description` left out is cleared
and a `userId` left out makes the profile a brand.

description.description: What the profile is for. Blank is the same as left out.

name.description:
The profile's name, handle-shaped: lowercase letters, digits, `-` or `_`, starting with a
letter or digit, at most 64 characters, never `all`, and not a name another visible profile uses. Trimmed and
lowercased before it is checked.

userId.description: The member of the organization the profile represents, as `org members` lists them. Null or left out for a brand.

ProfilePlatformStatus.description:
What `profile status` knows of one profile on one platform: whether it holds credentials (null when
the store could not answer), the names of the credential keys present (never their values), the
browser session on disk and whether a process holds it, roster membership, the last check, and the
status of the profile's mapped account in your Blowhorn account.

account_status.description:
The status of the profile's one mapped account (a connection in your Blowhorn account) on this platform,
such as connected or disconnected; conflict when two are mapped; null when none is mapped or the
accounts could not be read (see the response's `accounts`). A connected account is what proves
the account is connected on every computer.

browser_session_mtime.description: When the session directory last changed.

credential_keys_present.description: The names of the platform credential keys that are set, never their values.

roster.description: Whether the roster lists the platform for the profile; null when the roster could not be read.

ProfilePlatformStatus.title: ProfilePlatformStatus

ProfileSessionCheck.description:
The last recorded session verdict for one profile and platform. Which optional keys appear depends
on the platform's probe: a GitHub check adds login, scopes, needs and limited; a browser check a url
(and a signed-in LinkedIn check the username it read);
a Slack check its workspaces; a busy session the pid holding it.

checked_at.description: Local time, formatted as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.

lock_pid.description: The process holding the browser session, on a busy verdict.

login.description: The account a token authenticated as.

needs.description: Scopes the token lacks for a command, each with the command named.

revision.description: The write order of the verdict, which says which of two checks in the same second is later.

scopes.description: The scopes a GitHub token holds.

url.description: The page a browser probe ended on.

username.description: The account name a signed-in browser session reads as its own, on a valid check that could read it: LinkedIn's profile name (the part after /in/), X's handle, Reddit's username, Hacker News's username.

workspaces.description: Per-workspace verdicts of a Slack check.

RunCounts.description: Summed action counts of a set of ledger records. For a scheduler tick record the counts are activities, not actions.

unconfirmed.description: Actions clicked whose outcome was never read.

RunCounts.title: RunCounts

ScheduleActivity.description:
One schedule activity as `schedule list` prints it - enough to explain the activity without a second
`schedule get`: why it is retrying, where its log is, who holds its lock and whether it is held.
Most values are the activity's text; `due`, `enabled` and `paused` are `yes` or `no`.

connection.description: The activity's Google Chrome connection, from the tick's gate (#1600): null when a run may start. `held` is a run that waits, not one that fails, with the plain reason and the one in-app action that clears it; `heal` is a connection Blowhorn reconnects on its own before the run; `open` is a mapped Google Chrome profile that is not open, which Blowhorn opens in the background before the run. Absent from older engines.

action.description: The one thing the person can do: `turn_on_extension` (turn the Blowhorn extension on in that Google Chrome profile), `reconnect` (reconnect it now), `choose_chrome_profile` (choose or confirm the Google Chrome profile) or `restart_chrome` (restart Google Chrome, the one action left when a native host process from before an upgrade is still answering and ending it did not clear the hold); null when Blowhorn heals it alone.

chrome_directory.description: The Google Chrome profile directory the activity's profile is mapped to; null when none is.

reason.description: Why it waits or reconnects, in plain words that name no command.

due.description: `yes` when the activity's time has come: it is enabled and valid, no machine holds a live claim on it, and its `next_run` has passed. Always `no` when `next_run` is empty. A paused activity still reads `yes`, and `paused` says the tick is holding it.

errors.description: Validation errors joined by a semicolon; empty when the activity is valid.

held_here.description: The claim is this install's own: this macOS user on this computer. Never decided by the hostname alone, which every macOS user on a Mac shares.

max_retries.description: The retry budget for each arming; see `Max Retries` in the activity's values.

next_run.description: When the tick next takes the activity, in local time. Empty when it never will: a completed once-only activity, or a completed or failed activity with no Next Run At. Never the activity's old Run At.

platform.description: The platform, or `all`.

profile.description: The profile, or a hyphen when the activity names none.

quiet_hours.description: `yes` when the activity is inside its quiet hours now (see `quiet_hours_window`): the tick holds it, unclaimed, and runs it when the window ends. Computed, never stored.

quiet_hours_tz.description: The zone `quiet_hours_window` is read in: an IANA name, or this computer's zone; empty when no window is set.

quiet_hours_until.description: When the current window ends, in local time; empty when the activity is not in quiet hours now.

quiet_hours_window.description: The quiet-hours window in force for the activity's profile, `HH:MM-HH:MM` like `22:00-07:00`; empty when no window is set anywhere for it.

retry_count.description: Failed attempts since the activity was last armed; see `Retry Count` in the activity's values.

risk_hold.description: Why a Run now would be held, including while the profile is warming up. Empty when the activity may run. A confirmation passes this hold except when `risk_hold_source` is `published`.

risk_hold_source.description: Where the hold comes from. `published` is a limit the platform states, which a confirmation does not pass. Empty when `risk_hold` is empty.

risk_profile.description: The preset the activity resolves to, from the tick's gate; empty for an activity without one profile and one platform, which names no single preset.

risk_profile_effective.description: What the tick enforces: cautious while warming, whatever was chosen; empty with `risk_profile`.

risk_profile_source.description: The layer that chose the preset (`schedule` when the activity's own value did, `builtin` when nothing chose one); empty with `risk_profile`.

risk_profile_warming.description: `yes` while the profile or this computer is warming up; empty with `risk_profile` (an activity on every platform names no single preset).

status.description: The activity's stored status, such as pending, scheduled, running, retrying or failed. Never a lock.

ScheduleHeartbeat.description:
The heartbeat the last scheduler pass wrote: when it ran, what it checked and claimed, and the
store cause if the pass met an outage. A heartbeat that could not be read is `{error, path}` instead.

next_due_at.description: The earliest instant an activity falls due after this pass, which the resident service wakes for; null when the pass did not reach the schedule.

skipped_cancelled.description: Row numbers a cancelled pass did not reach.

skipped_paused.description: Row numbers left unclaimed because a pause held them.

stop.description: The organization-wide stop as the pass last saw it, or null.

stopped.description: Whether the organization-wide stop ended the pass; a stopped pass is also cancelled.

store_cause.description: The named cause beside `store_error` (schema_behind, tunnel_refused and so on); null when the pass reached the store. Absent in heartbeats written before the field existed.

ScheduleStatusResponse.description:
Prints the scheduler at a glance: whether this machine is paused, the last pass's heartbeat and
whether passes are still running (`stalled` is true when none has run lately), today's run counts,
the store as the last pass saw it (never a probe) and the background service's state. There is no
countdown: the service runs when something is due, and re-scans at least every minute.

last_tick.description: The last pass's heartbeat; null when no pass has run.

service.description:
The background service, on macOS. When its state cannot be read (any platform but macOS, or
a launchd read that failed) the command still exits 0 and this is a Problem naming why.

stalled.description: True when the last heartbeat is too old for a service that re-scans every minute, so no pass has run lately on this machine.

available.description: Null when no pass has said either way.

cause.description: The named cause beside `error` (schema_behind, tunnel_refused and so on); null when the last pass reached the store or no pass has said either way.

today.description: Today's pass counts from the run ledger; null without a log directory.

ScheduleValues.description:
A schedule row's columns, each a string (empty when unset): the command and its params as
`key=value;key=value`, when it runs and how it repeats, its retry budget, its status and the lock a
running machine holds.

Max Retries.description: The retry budget for each arming: how many times a failed run is retried before the row is failed. Raising it alone does not schedule a failed row again.

Next Run At.description: When the row is next due, in local time. Empty on a completed or failed row means never due again. An update that gives a completed or failed row a Next Run At, or changes its Run At, schedules it again in the same write: Status scheduled and Retry Count 0, with Last Run At, Last Error and Last Log Path kept, unless the update sets Status itself.

Retry Count.description: Failed attempts since the row was last armed. A success sets it to 0, and so does an update that schedules a completed or failed row again.

Risk Profile.description: The activity's own Risk Profile (#1009): `cautious`, `standard` or `brisk`, or empty to inherit the preset its profile and platform resolve to.

claim.description: The activity's lease - claimed, by, at, lease_expires_at, stale, this_machine.

due.description: Whether the activity's time has come, read from the same instant schedule list prints as next_run. The claim and the pauses are rungs of their own.

due_at.description: That instant in local time. Empty when the activity is never due again (a completed once-only activity, or a completed or failed activity with no Next Run At) or has no Run At.

quiet_hours.description: The quiet hours in force for the activity's profile; null when no window is set anywhere for it.

held.description: Whether the activity is inside the window now.

source.description: Whether the window came from the profile's own Quiet Hours setting or the defaults.

tz.description: The zone the window is read in: an IANA name, or this computer's zone.

until.description: When the window ends, as an instant in its zone; null when not held.

until_clock.description: That ending as the zone's wall clock, `HH:MM`; null when not held.

risk.description: The activity's Risk Profile (#1009): its own setting (empty when it inherits), the preset it effectively runs, and where that preset came from (`schedule` for its own setting).

this_machine.description: This machine's host, last tick (the heartbeat's name for its last pass), store state, and whether passes are still running (passing).

rung.description: The first rung that stopped the activity.

up_to_date.description: Null when nothing is installed or the installed file could not be compared.

SessionAccount.description:
What Blowhorn recorded for one of a profile's accounts (a connection mapped to the profile)
in your Blowhorn account. Confirming a Chrome profile records each attached platform's username as
the account's name, at its account page when the username is a handle: the account is
registered and mapped (created) or takes the new name and page (updated). A session check
on a browser platform (LinkedIn, X or Reddit) registers the account (created), raises it
back to connected (reconnected), or marks a sign-in that ended disconnected. Nothing is
deleted. A connection the profile opted out of is left as it stands (unchanged).

outcome.description: none - not signed in and no account is mapped, so nothing was written.

UpgradeRequest.description: The flags and arguments of `blowhorn upgrade`, one property per parameter.

chrome_launch.description: How this run reaches Google Chrome, for one run: 'extension' (the default) drives Chrome through the Blowhorn Chrome extension and starts no Playwright Chrome; 'persistent' launches Blowhorn's own Chrome from chrome.automation_data_dir with the mapped profile directory inside it; 'cdp' attaches to a running Chrome that is ready per 'blowhorn chrome status' (daily Chrome asks you to Allow once per connection; a dedicated attach-chrome started with 'blowhorn chrome attach-chrome start' does not); and 'auto' attaches when Chrome is ready and launches otherwise. This flag, then BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, then BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, then defaults.chrome.launch_mode in .blowhorn.yaml, selects the driver a run actually uses. Any other value is refused before anything runs. Every browser run needs the profile mapped with 'blowhorn chrome map' first, in any mode. A scheduler tick's jobs each resolve their own mode (this flag on the tick, BLOWHORN_CHROME_LAUNCH, the job's driver mode, BLOWHORN_BROWSER_DRIVER, defaults.chrome.launch_mode, then the extension)

exclude.description: Profiles to exclude when using --profile all (comma delimited); alias: --e; use 'none' or an empty string to clear configured defaults

headed.description: Keep the browser window visible and in front (overrides --headless) so a person can finish a sign-in or challenge

headless.description: Run unattended in a background browser window: never headless (Chrome would announce the run as HeadlessChrome to every site) and no waiting for a person at a sign-in or challenge. When the run attaches to your running Chrome (--chrome-launch cdp, or auto while 'blowhorn chrome status' says ready) the tab opens in its own visible Chrome window instead: a hidden tab is throttled, so the previous app is only re-activated once

UpgradeResponse.description: The upgrade report: whether this Mac's local data was carried from an earlier version's home into the home this version uses, and what each step carried. source.description: The earlier home data was carried from, or null when none was found.

status.description: upgraded (steps applied and recorded), planned (a dry run: nothing written, the upgrade is still due), current (nothing to carry), busy (a pass is running from the earlier home; nothing was touched), failed (a step failed or the record would not parse; nothing was recorded for the failed step).

reason.description: Why a not-run step did not run.

status.description: not-run when the earlier home was refused (it belongs to another macOS user); reason says why and nothing was carried.

UrlClassification.description:
What `blowhorn classify-url <url> --json` says a link is (issue #1839): the menu-bar popover's
drop reads it to choose its sheet. The engine decides it from the platform rules it already keeps
(`engine/blowhorn/url_classify.py`, the predicates each platform module acts on), so the desktop
app keeps no copy of them. `post` is an existing post or comment on a supported platform, with the
verbs that platform takes; `page` is any other web link, with the platform whose site it is on
(Hacker News items are pages: they take no engage verb); `none` is anything that is not a web link.
Nothing here names a person, an account or a secret.

kind.description: post (engage with it), page (a new order that uses the page) or none (not a web link).

platform.description: The platform the link names, or null when it names none.

url.description: The link as it was given, trimmed.

verbs.description: The engage verbs a post takes, in the order the sheet offers them; empty for a page and for a platform with none.

WithdrawResponse.description:
What `blowhorn withdraw --json` prints on exit 0: the sent invitations the
run examined as profile URLs, how many withdrawals it confirmed, and how
many cards it left alone. A row never carries a display name: identity is
the profile URL only, so no person's name lands in a committed artifact.
`--limit` is spent only on confirmed withdrawals: a click that reads no
confirmation neither consumes the budget nor counts as withdrawn, and a
combined unconfirmed/failed streak halts the run. A card whose age cannot be
parsed is always kept and counted under `unreadable`, never withdrawn. On a
dry run `sent` is 0 and `candidates` are the eligible rows `--apply` would
withdraw.

candidates.description: The eligible sent invitations the run examined, as profile URLs, oldest first as the list renders them.

profile_url.description: The invitee's LinkedIn profile URL. Never a display name.

dry_run.description: True when nothing was withdrawn and nothing was written.

examined.description: Cards examined, including cards left alone.

failed.description: Cards whose withdrawal failed after the control was clicked.

held.description: Rows held as clicked with the outcome not read. Withdrawal records none of its own; the list is empty unless a held row was carried in.

sent.description: Withdrawals confirmed (the card provably left the sent list). Always 0 on a dry run.

skipped.description: Cards examined and left alone (too new to withdraw, or an age that could not be parsed).

too_new.description: Cards newer than the `--older-than` cutoff, left alone.

unconfirmed.description: Cards clicked whose withdrawal could not be confirmed from the list.

unreadable.description: Cards whose pending age could not be parsed, kept and never withdrawn.

withdrawn.description: Withdrawals confirmed, the same count as `sent`.

WithdrawResponse.title: WithdrawResponse

post.description:
Show or set whether your account shares anonymous usage data for product improvement.

Reads and writes anonymousUsageStats in your Blowhorn account's preferences (GET /api/identity/users/profile, PUT /api/identity/users/preferences with that one field, so no other preference changes). It belongs to the account, so every computer you use Blowhorn on follows it. Not set reads as on. Usage data is anonymous counts of what Blowhorn does; it never carries a post's text, a message, a credential or the contents of a page Blowhorn drives. Failure reports are a separate setting in the desktop app. With no flag it reads your account and always exits 0: signed out or unreachable, it reports the setting last read for this account (or on) and says why. --on and --off save the setting and exit 1 when your account cannot be written. --dry-run reads and sends nothing.

post.description:
Sign in to Blowhorn at https://cloud.blowhorn.ai in your browser.

Opens https://cloud.blowhorn.ai, where you sign in or create an account and allow the Blowhorn app, then returns here and keeps the token in the macOS Keychain (elsewhere a file only you can read beside cloud.yaml). It uses Blowhorn's native client sign-in: the browser answers on 127.0.0.1 with a one-time code this command redeems with a PKCE verifier; there is no client secret, and the token is never printed. After sign-in it reads your plan once; an account without a Blowhorn plan is sent straight to https://cloud.blowhorn.ai to start the beta. --no-browser prints the sign-in address instead of opening it; --json opens no browser either, its first line names the address to open (the desktop app runs --no-browser --json and opens it itself). --dry-run names where it would sign in and opens, waits for and saves nothing.

post.description: Ask the Chrome extension for the front tab's address and title, through the bridge, and print it. The popover's New order asks here first: it retries briefly and never uses Apple Events, so macOS never prompts for Chrome. If the live read has no tab, a reachable extension may return its last remembered normal-window HTTP(S) tab with stale and age fields. This command navigates nowhere, probes no tab's page, and contacts no platform: it reads only the front tab's own address and title, from the Chrome profile whose bridge answers first. No reachable extension or no live or remembered tab answers with no tab, and --json carries connected and a detail saying why. That read writes nothing but the bridge lock, the same lock `chrome extension-status` writes. --json emits the answer as one object, for a script or the desktop app.

post.description:
Start or report a dedicated Chrome that is open to remote debugging with no Allow dialog, so '--chrome-launch cdp' can attach to a real Chrome unattended. Chrome 136 and later ignore '--remote-debugging-port' on the default data directory, which is why this is a second Chrome on a tree of its own (~/.blowhorn/attach-chrome, on a port Chrome picks and records, bound to 127.0.0.1) and never your daily one. That port has no password and asks for no Allow, and loopback is shared by every macOS user on this Mac, so any other user signed in here can control that Chrome, its cookies and signed-in sessions included. That is why it is off by default: 'start' and 'install-agent' refuse without --allow-other-users. Sign it in only to the accounts Blowhorn posts from.

'status' (the default) reads that tree's 'Local State', 'DevToolsActivePort' and 'SingletonLock' and nothing else -- no browser opens, nothing connects -- and its last line says what to do next. 'signin' opens the tree with no remote debugging at all, for the one-time sign-in to each account Blowhorn posts from, because some sites (Google among them) refuse to sign in inside a browser started with debugging on; quit that Chrome when you are done and the sign-ins carry over. 'stop' quits the Chrome holding the tree the way Cmd-Q does (DevTools Browser.close, so fresh sign-ins are saved), waits, then sends SIGTERM; it signals only that Chrome and never SIGKILLs. 'install-agent' adds a per-user LaunchAgent (ai.blowhorn.attach-chrome) that runs 'start' once at each login, so scheduler ticks find it up, and 'uninstall-agent' removes it (the Chrome keeps running). 'start' launches Chrome on the tree, detached, with the port open, and prints the steps that finish the setup: point chrome.data_dir at the tree, map your profiles, then run with '--chrome-launch cdp'. It writes no configuration of its own. The tree is fixed and Chrome picks the port, so its one option of its own is the opt-in. A recorded port is evidence a Chrome is up on that tree, not proof a connect would succeed, and it counts only while a live Chrome holds the tree. Starting is refused when the tree is Google Chrome's own default data directory (never the one chrome.data_dir names, which step 1 above points at this tree), when a live Chrome already has a port recorded there, and while the tree is open without debugging (the signin window): quit that Chrome first. A port file a crashed Chrome left behind is cleared, not refused. --dry-run prints the command line and starts nothing.

post.description:
Apply the confirm screen's confirmed choices: turn Chrome profiles into Blowhorn profiles, attach the discovered platform accounts, and map each Chrome profile -- the one write onboarding makes, and the person's confirm is the consent it records. The choices arrive as one JSON document on stdin (--payload-stdin), so a GitHub token or a Bluesky app password in it reaches neither argv nor the daily log:

  {"assignments": [{"directory": "Profile 3", "profile": "ada-example", "create": true,
     "userId": "<the member's uuid, as 'org members' lists them; omit it for a brand>",
     "platforms": {"linkedin": {"attach": true, "session": true}, "x": {"attach": true},
       "github": {"attach": true, "token": "..."}, "bluesky": {"attach": true, "app_password": "..."},
       "slack": {"attach": true}}}]}

Per assignment, in order: the Blowhorn profile (an existing one the payload names by 'profileId' or by 'profile', the one the directory is already mapped to, or, with "create": true, a new one created in your Blowhorn account representing the member 'userId' names, or nobody for a brand; a name the payload omits is proposed from the Google name, and a profile the organization does not have is never created without "create"); then the attached platforms' credentials, stored in your Blowhorn account and nowhere on this computer; then the mapping, exactly as 'chrome map' records it and, when the extension is already on in that Chrome profile, paired the same way, opening the extension's pairing page there, since a run refuses a mapping the extension cannot prove; a profile without the extension on yet is paired once it is (the desktop's setup does this, or 'chrome map'); then each attached platform's username as the profile's account there: a connection registered and linked to the profile, named for the username and pointing at its account page when the username is a handle, which is where the profile's handles are read from. A platform row the payload marks with "session": true (LinkedIn, Hacker News) stores a confirmed-session credential naming this Chrome profile directory instead of a password: it satisfies eligibility the way a session-capture platform's identity key does, because the run checks that Chrome session before it reaches for a password. GitHub stores GH_USERNAME and still waits for GH_TOKEN; Bluesky stores the handle and still waits for the app password; both may ride in the same payload. Slack stores nothing: its session is captured afterwards by 'profile auth --platform slack', and the result says so.

A profile the document marks with "in_use": false is recorded not in use: this computer's mapping for that directory is removed, the Blowhorn profile is added to defaults.exclude when that name is not already there, and the profile and its credentials are kept. A platform row with "attach": false is recorded not in use for that profile in .blowhorn.chrome-not-in-use.json beside the config file; a platform left out of the assignment is left as it was recorded. The credential is kept, and a later run on this computer skips a platform still recorded not in use. Marking a platform in use clears that skip for the Blowhorn profile on every Chrome directory in the record, so a later choice in the same document wins. Marking the profile in use again removes it from defaults.exclude only when this screen added that name; a name already in the list is left as written, spelling and notes included. Omitting "in_use" applies only the attached rows, as before.

Each assignment answers for itself in the result -- profile, whether it was created, the keys written per platform, the mapping, the accounts recorded, or the one-sentence refusal -- so a partial confirm is a successful confirm: what landed stays landed, and what refused says why, by name. The exit code is 0 when at least one assignment landed and 1 when none did; a store that cannot be reached is the named cause and exit 3. With --dry-run every check runs and nothing is written, created or mapped.

post.description:
Report, for every Chrome profile, the platform accounts discovery can see there -- the read behind onboarding's confirm screen. For each profile: its directory, display name and signed-in Google account (from 'Local State', as 'chrome profiles' reads them), the Blowhorn profile it is mapped to, the platform rows discovery found, a proposed Blowhorn profile slug, whether that slug is free, and how the Google email resolves against the organization's Blowhorn users.

A platform row is a saved-login username and whether a session is live. The usernames come from the profile's 'Login Data' and 'Login Data For Account', for an allowlist of hosts only (linkedin.com, x.com and twitter.com, reddit.com, news.ycombinator.com, github.com, bsky.app and bsky.social, slack.com): only the realm and the username are ever selected -- the password column is a blob Chrome encrypts, and it is never selected, decrypted or copied. Whether a session is live comes from cookie names in 'Cookies' or 'Network/Cookies': presence only, never a value, except GitHub's 'dotcom_user', whose value is the login name itself and so is the GitHub username when a session is live. Hacker News's 'user' cookie is not read at all: its value bundles the username with a session secret. History and LevelDB are never opened -- a visit is not an identity. No browser opens, and a file Chrome holds locked reads as 'not found', never as an error. Nothing is written to Chrome. For each Chrome profile mapped here and in use, whose identity holds, a LinkedIn, X or Reddit sign-in it is picked for is recorded as that profile's account in your Blowhorn account, and a sign-in that ended marks the account disconnected; nothing is deleted, and --local and --dry-run record nothing. A not-in-use row for a directory Chrome no longer has is dropped from the record beside the config file.

The resolution answers the create rule without creating: 'one' (the email names exactly one Blowhorn user in the organization; that user's Cloud social links ride along, shown on the confirm screen but never treated as permission to post), 'several' (the member candidates, for a picker), 'none' (no member holds the email), or 'no-email' (nobody is signed in to that Chrome profile). --json emits the whole survey with a stable shape, for the desktop app. A store that cannot be reached is the named cause and exit 3; an unreadable profile list is one sentence and exit 1.

--local reads Chrome's files only and never opens the store, so it works before sign-in: every row's mapping is null, its resolution is 'unresolved' (or 'no-email') and its slug state 'unchecked'. The desktop app runs it when it first opens, then merges the full survey once you are signed in. Chrome's Guest and System profiles are never listed.

post.description:
Write the native-messaging host manifest Chrome launches for the Blowhorn Chrome extension, and print where the unpacked extension lives so you can load it. The manifest is com.blowhorn.chrome_extension.json under Chrome's NativeMessagingHosts directory (~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/NativeMessagingHosts on macOS, ~/.config/google-chrome/NativeMessagingHosts on Linux), named com.blowhorn.chrome_extension, type stdio, path an executable launcher chrome_extension-host in Blowhorn's directory (~/Library/Application Support/Blowhorn on macOS, ~/.local/share/blowhorn on Linux) that runs the Python native-host program by default, or the Rust host with --native-host rust, and allowed_origins naming the extension id from the key in extension/manifest.json, the Chrome Web Store id and the older unpacked id. If you already installed the host, run this command again and reload the extension once. A missing key or an unreadable extension manifest is one sentence and nothing is written; --dry-run prints both paths and the manifest and writes nothing. This command does not launch Chrome and does not load the extension.

--profile <name> names the Blowhorn profile whose mapped Chrome profile should get the extension (resolved through 'blowhorn chrome map' on this machine); --chrome-profile '<directory>' names the Chrome profile directory itself, as 'blowhorn chrome profiles' prints it, and can be given more than once. Either one writes the native host as above, checks the directory is in Chrome's Local State, and prints the steps to load the extension in that profile alone: Chrome has no file this command can write that installs an extension in one profile only, since the policy and the external-extensions file both reach every profile. A profile with no mapping, a directory Chrome does not have, and either flag with --all-profiles are one sentence and nothing is written; a store that cannot be reached is the named cause and exit 3. A --profile inherited from BLOWHORN_PROFILE or defaults.profile does not count.

--all-profiles also asks Chrome to install that extension in every Chrome profile on this machine. It is every Chrome profile, not --profile all. The default route writes ExtensionInstallForcelist: silent, every profile, Chrome shows Managed by your organization, and macOS may ask for an administrator password once. On macOS that policy is your own user's, never the computer's, so other macOS users' Chrome is left alone. On Linux the policy file (/etc/opt/chrome/policies/managed/blowhorn.json) and the external file (/usr/share/google-chrome/extensions/<id>.json) need root, Blowhorn never asks for it, and a write this user cannot make is refused with the file, its exact content and the sudo command that writes that one file. Never run this command under sudo: the host and launcher would land under root's home, which your Chrome never reads, so a run under sudo is refused by name. --external writes Chrome's external-extensions file instead, so Chrome offers the install in each profile, one click there, and does not show that banner. --external without --all-profiles is refused and writes nothing. Switching route removes the other route's file for this extension id. Both routes name the extension id from that same key and the Chrome Web Store update url; Chrome can fetch the extension only once that id is published. A policy file that exists and cannot be read is one sentence and nothing is written. Per-profile lines say what Chrome was asked to do, never that a profile's copy was confirmed. Those lines cover the configured Chrome data directory. The policy route applies the extension to every Chrome profile on this machine. --json appends one trailing object (manifest, launcher, extension_dir, removed), for a script or the desktop app. With --all-profiles that object also carries route, extension_id, profiles, profiles_error and profiles_scope; with --profile or --chrome-profile it carries targets. --ensure, with exactly one --profile or --chrome-profile, ensures the extension for that profile the way a run does on demand: it repairs the native host when missing or stale, registers the extension for that profile's data directory when nothing is there yet, and re-probes hello once. A profile already carrying a Chrome Web Store install is left alone, and a store install too old for this Blowhorn is reported with Chrome's own update step, never forced. --ensure refuses --all-profiles and --external, writes nothing with --dry-run, and never starts, restarts, or kills Chrome.

--native-host rust points the same launcher at the Rust native host instead of the Python one: the launcher execs engine/rust/target/release/blowhorn-host in this checkout (built with 'cargo build --release -p blowhorn-host' in engine/rust), or the binary --rust-host names. It is off by default. A Rust host that is missing or not executable is one sentence, nothing is written, and the installed launcher stays as it is. The choice is kept in the launcher itself: a later install or --ensure with no --native-host, the desktop app's automatic one included, keeps the Rust host while its binary is still executable, and puts the Python launcher back, saying so, once it is not. --native-host python switches back. --json carries native_host, python or rust, and native_host_fallback, the sentence when the Rust host was replaced.

post.description: Show or set how runs drive the Blowhorn Chrome extension. background is the default. Both modes open Blowhorn's tab inactive beside the tab you are on (or in its own window with --window own-window), in a Blowhorn group that is collapsed by default, and take a screenshot through the debugger without selecting the tab. Nothing brings the tab forward. classic keeps focus emulation on only while an action holds the debugger and sends input through the page. background turns focus emulation on from the first page and sends trusted input. With no MODE it reports the mode a run started now would use and where it comes from: the BLOWHORN_EXTENSION_ROLLBACK override, your Blowhorn account setting, or the background default. A job whose driver mode is extension-classic or extension-background outranks the account setting for that job. Setting MODE writes extensionMode to your account's Blowhorn preferences in your Blowhorn account (sign in first with 'blowhorn auth login'); default clears it. --group collapsed or open writes chromeGroup the same way: how the Blowhorn tab group sits beside your tabs between steps. Collapsed is the default. --window side-tab or own-window writes chromeWindow the same way: where Blowhorn works. side-tab is an inactive tab beside your tabs, the default. own-window is one window of its own, mostly behind yours with an edge showing, opened without focus and reused for the browser session; on a Mac keep that edge showing, since a window fully covered, minimized, hidden or on another desktop reads like a background tab. --json emits the report as one object, for a script or the desktop app.

post.description: Report whether the Blowhorn Chrome extension is installed and connected: the unpacked extension directory, the native-host manifest (missing, current, or stale against this checkout's extension/manifest.json), the launcher, and whether the Chrome extension answers hello on its socket. An answered hello proves the extension is loaded in the real Chrome and talking; this command navigates nowhere, probes no tab, and contacts no platform. A manifest whose launcher is gone is not installed. The report also says which install route is on disk: policy (ExtensionInstallForcelist, every Chrome profile, Managed by your organization), external (Chrome offers the install in each profile), or none. That read writes nothing. Which Chrome profile accepted that install is not something this command can see. It does name each Chrome profile whose Secure Preferences or Preferences record a Chrome Web Store install of the extension, with its version, and tells a store install too old for this Blowhorn to update in chrome://extensions, never to load it unpacked. The one thing written is a lock beside each Chrome profile's own socket, in Blowhorn's directory (~/Library/Application Support/Blowhorn on macOS, ~/.local/share/blowhorn on Linux), which every Blowhorn client holds while it talks to that profile's Chrome extension: while a run holds one profile's lock, that profile's hello is not written, is reported not checked, and --json carries bridge_busy: true with a detail saying a run may be holding the bridge; another profile's run never waits on it. --json emits the report as one object, for a script or the desktop app.

post.description:
Map a Blowhorn profile to one of this machine's Chrome profiles, by the Chrome profile's directory name as 'blowhorn chrome profiles' prints it ('Default', 'Profile 12'). The command checks that the Blowhorn profile is in the store, that Chrome has that directory (Chrome silently creates a new, empty profile for a directory it does not know, so a typo is refused rather than recorded), and that the directory is not already mapped to another Blowhorn profile on this machine; then it records the display name and signed-in account Chrome shows for the directory and prints what it recorded. A Blowhorn profile may have several Chrome profiles mapped on one machine (Work and Personal, say), so mapping another directory adds it; mapping a directory the profile already has refreshes the recorded identity, which is how a drifted name or account is confirmed. A Chrome profile belongs to one Blowhorn profile per machine. --replace removes the profile's other mappings on this machine in the same write.

Which Chrome profile a run uses, per platform: the one mapped --for that platform; else the profile's only mapping; else its one mapping with no --for (its default, which serves every platform no other mapping names). With several mappings and none of those, the run refuses by name. --for linkedin,x chooses this Chrome profile for those platforms and takes them off the profile's other mappings here; --default clears this mapping's platforms; neither keeps what the mapping had.

A mapping is identity, never permission: it does not make a profile eligible for anything; every browser run reads it to find the profile's Chrome and refuses a profile without one.

Mapping also pairs the profile: once the mapping is recorded the command asks Chrome to open a window on the Blowhorn extension's pairing page in that Chrome profile, carrying a token made from this machine's pairing key (chrome_pairing.key in Blowhorn's launcher directory, created on first use and readable only by you). The page keeps the token in the extension's storage, and a run through the extension refuses before any action unless the extension it reaches reports this profile's token. Mapping a profile to the directory it already has pairs it again. When Chrome cannot be asked to open the page the mapping still stands and the command says why and what to run. --json adds 'pairing': opened (whether Chrome was asked to open the page) and detail (why not, or null). With --dry-run the command checks everything, records nothing and opens no pairing page. Each refusal is one sentence and exit 1; a store that cannot be reached is the named cause and exit 3.

post.description: Open a window in the Chrome profile a Blowhorn profile is mapped to on this machine, so you can look at it or sign in to a platform there yourself. The mapping decides which Chrome profile opens, by the same rule a run uses: with --sign-in, the mapping chosen for that platform; without it, the profile's only mapping or its default one. A profile with no mapping here, a mapping Chrome no longer has, or a name or account that drifted since the mapping was made is refused by name and nothing opens -- a mapping is identity, never a guess at another profile. With --sign-in <platform> the window opens on that platform's sign-in page; without it, on a new tab. post.description:
Sweep a repository's assigned-but-stalled issues through GitHub's GraphQL API.

For each assignee whose silence -- measured from the later of their assignment date and their last activity (a comment, a linked PR, a status change) -- reaches --nudge-after-days (default 14), the action posts a fixed-template nudge; --warn-after-days (default 7) later with still no reply it posts a final warning; --unassign-after-days (default 7) after that it removes the assignee and posts a closing comment. Issues with an open linked PR from the assignee, blocked or waiting-on-maintainer labels, security labels, or an assignee who is the issue's own author are never bumped. A dry run is the default: without --apply the sweep prints exactly what it would do and writes nothing. Immediately before any write the issue is re-read, so a run never unassigns someone who just became active. No CLI is required: the sweep talks to GitHub's GraphQL API over HTTPS with the store's GitHub token, and a token that is missing or unauthenticated is a hard error, never a silent fallback.

post.description:
Refresh authentication/session state for one or more platforms.

Supported platforms and authentication mechanisms:

  linkedin  - Persistent browser session. Automated login via
              LI_USERNAME / LI_PASSWORD in the store,
              with fallback to manual browser entry.

  x         - Persistent browser session. Automated login via
              X_USERNAME / X_PASSWORD in the store,
              with fallback to manual browser entry.

  reddit    - Persistent browser session. Automated login via
              RDDT_USERNAME / RDDT_PASSWORD in the store,
              with fallback to manual browser entry.

  slack     - Hybrid: session credentials (xoxc token + d cookie)
              captured through the run's browser driver (the
              extension by default), saved to the profile's Slack
              credential in the store, and
              reused for direct API calls. No Slack app install
              required. Use --workspace <host> to capture a new
              workspace; omit it to refresh every workspace listed
              under 'slack_workspaces' in that credential. Use
              --mode paste for the legacy OAuth-token flow.

  bluesky   - No browser. Logs in to Bluesky with a handle and app
              password -- the same login every post makes -- and
              stores the pair only when Bluesky accepts it, so a
              refused credential is never saved. For one named
              profile in a terminal it asks for both (the stored
              handle is the default; a blank app password keeps the
              stored one); --handle and --app-password-stdin supply
              them without a prompt. Otherwise the stored pair is
              logged in with and nothing is written.

Use --profile all to refresh every profile in your organization after
applying any --exclude filters. The profiles are read from the store; a
store that cannot be reached is the named cause and exit 3.

With --headless the browser still opens, as a background window (Chrome is
never run headless); only automated credential login is attempted and the
manual browser fallback is skipped.

post.description:
Store KEY=VALUE pairs on a profile: its platform credentials and its run settings.
A platform key (LI_*, X_*, RDDT_*, HN_*, SLACK_*, BLUESKY_*, GH_*, YT_*, IG_*, FB_*,
TIKTOK_*, slack_workspaces and the <WORKSPACE>_SLACK_* session keys) is stored in that
platform's credential in the store, where runs read it. A run setting (Risk Profile,
Risk Profile By Platform, Daily Caps, Quiet Hours, Quiet Hours Time Zone) is stored in
the profile's settings in your Blowhorn account, and a value a run could not read is
refused. A blank value clears a key. Any other key is refused, and every refusal comes
before anything is sent. Nothing is written to a file. The output names the keys that
changed and never echoes a value.
Replacing a credential an API check judges (GH_TOKEN, the Bluesky handle or app
password, a Slack token or captured session) sets that platform back to not
checked in profile status until the next check, because each such check records
which credential it judged. A browser platform's check is about its saved session
and stays.

A profile is created with profile create, and who it represents changes with
profile update.

post.description:
Report what each profile in your organization is set up for: the platforms it holds
an account for (credential key names only -- values are never printed), the browser
session directory and its last-modified time, whether another blowhorn process holds
its lock, the last recorded session check, and whether the profile is excluded by
default. The profiles are your organization's list in your Blowhorn account, read
once; a store that cannot be reached is the named cause and exit 3. No browser and
no platform network by default: accounts are read from the store's credentials,
once for every profile, with the person each profile represents. A credential read
the store fails leaves every account unknown and is named on a Credentials: line,
not fatal, and a check made then skips every platform and keeps its last results.
With --json each platform also carries account_status: the status of the
profile's account in your Blowhorn account (connected, disconnected, ...), read
once for every profile, or null when none is mapped.

--check-sessions runs a read-only probe per configured platform (LinkedIn, X and
Reddit open the saved session in a background window and look for the signed-in
page; GitHub,
Bluesky and Slack call their APIs) and records the result in the profile's
session_status.json under data/cache/profiles/, and records a LinkedIn, X or Reddit
sign-in it finds (or one that ended) on the profile's account in your Blowhorn
account. It never logs in, never types a
credential, and reports 'busy' instead of waiting when a session is in use.
--check-platform runs that same probe for one platform only and leaves every
other platform's recorded result alone; --check-platform github checks the
profile's GitHub token in the store against GitHub (the login it signs in as,
its scopes and what they lack) with no browser at all.
--roster additionally reads the profiles roster from the store to show which
platforms each profile has a handle for; a store that cannot be reached is
the named cause and exit 3, and a roster that reads empty or cannot be read
is reported on a Roster: line, not fatal.
--chrome additionally reads this machine's Chrome profile mappings from the
store, once, and Chrome's own profile list, and adds a Chrome column: the
mapped Chrome profile directory and whether the name and account recorded
when it was mapped still match (drift, missing, unknown). A mapping is
identity, never permission. A Chrome profile list that cannot be read is
reported on a Chrome: line, not fatal.

post.description:
Replace the fields a person sets on one profile.
The profile is named by its name or its id, and the fields come from the JSON
document on stdin (--payload-stdin): name (required), description and userId. The
document is the whole of them: a description left out is cleared, and a userId left
out makes the profile a brand that represents nobody. The profile's run settings
(Risk Profile, caps, quiet hours) are read just before the write and sent back as
they are, and its owner is unchanged. The same refusals as `profile create` apply,
a rename onto another profile's name included; --dry-run sends nothing.
